lessons.title: if/else traps
lessons.summary: No truthiness, = vs ==, dangling else and unreachable code.

blocks.text: An `if` (and `while`, `for`, `do`) condition must have type **boolean**. Nothing else converts to true or false.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python treats `0`, `""`, `[]` and `None` as false. Java has **no truthiness**: `if (n)` with an `int` is a compile error, not a check for zero.
`=` assigns and the expression's value is the assigned value. That value must be boolean for `if` to accept it.

blocks.title: Assignment with a boolean
blocks.text: `if (b = true)` compiles and always takes the branch. When an exam condition uses a single `=`, check the variable's type: `int` means *Compilation fails*, `boolean` means it runs and changes the variable.

steps.explanation: `done = true` assigns `true` to `done`, and the whole expression has the value `true`, so the `if` branch runs. `done` stays `true` afterwards. It compiles because `done` is a `boolean`.

steps.prompt: Given `int n = 3; boolean ok = false; String s = "";`, which two conditions compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `ok = n > 2` assigns a boolean to a boolean variable, so its value is boolean. `!ok` is boolean. `n`, `n = 3` (an `int`) and `s` (a `String`) are not booleans, and Java never converts them.

blocks.text: Without braces, an `if` controls exactly **one** statement. An `else` always belongs to the **nearest** unmatched `if`, whatever the indentation says.

blocks.title: Ignore the indentation
blocks.text: On the exam, re-indent the code in your head by pairing each `else` with the closest `if` before it that has no `else` yet. Java does not read whitespace.

steps.explanation: The `else` pairs with the nearest `if`, which is `if (x > 2)`. That whole inner `if/else` is the body of `if (x > 10)`. Since `x > 10` is false, neither A nor B prints; only `C` does.

blocks.text: The compiler rejects any statement it can prove will **never run**. The rules are specific; memorize this table.

blocks.title: Why is if (false) allowed?
blocks.text: Java deliberately allows `if (false)` so you can switch debug code off with a constant flag. Loops get no such exception.

blocks.title: if/else that always returns
blocks.text: If **both** branches of an `if/else` end in `return`, any statement after it is unreachable and the method does not compile.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that causes the compile error.
steps.explanation: `while (false)` makes the loop body unreachable, and an unreachable statement is a compile error. `if (false)` on line 2 is the one allowed exception, so lines 2 to 4 compile.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Both branches of the `if/else` return, so the `if/else` can never complete normally. `return 0;` on line 5 is unreachable, which is a compile error. Without the `else`, it would compile and print `1`.

lessons.title: switch statements
lessons.summary: Legal types, constant labels, fall-through and default.

blocks.text: Wrappers are unboxed before matching. That means a `null` `Integer` or `String` selector throws a **NullPointerException**.

blocks.title: Coming in Unit 4
blocks.text: Java 21 also lets you switch on any object with **type patterns** (`case String s ->`, `case null ->`). That's pattern matching, covered in Unit 4. Here we stick to constant labels.
Each `case` value must be a **compile-time constant** that fits the selector type, and no value may appear twice.

items: `final` variables initialized with a constant: `final int A = 1;` then `case A:`

blocks.title: final is not enough
blocks.text: `final int C; C = 3;` is final but **not** a compile-time constant, because it isn't initialized in its declaration. Also: `byte b` with `case 128:` fails (128 doesn't fit in a byte), and duplicate labels fail.

steps.prompt: Given `final int A = 1; int b = 2; final int C; C = 3;` and `switch (n)` where `n` is an `int`, which two labels compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `A` is final and initialized with a constant, and `2 + 2` is a constant expression. `b` is not final, `C` is assigned after its declaration, and a method call is never a compile-time constant.

blocks.text: In a colon-style switch, a `case` label is only an **entry point**. After jumping there, execution keeps running into the following cases until a `break` or the closing brace.

blocks.caption: Prints ab

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python's `match` runs exactly one case. Java's colon-style `switch` falls through by default. Missing `break` is the classic exam trap.

steps.explanation: Execution enters at `case 2`, prints `two `, falls through into `case 3` and prints `three `, then `break` leaves the switch. `four` is never reached.

blocks.text: `default` may appear at the top, middle or bottom. It's used only when **no** case matches, but once entered, it falls through like any other label.

blocks.caption: Prints D1

steps.explanation: No case matches 9, so execution jumps to `default` (even though it's first), prints `D`, then falls through into `case 1` and `case 2` until the `break`.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `long` is not a legal switch type for constant labels (neither are `float`, `double` and `boolean`). The code does not compile.

steps.prompt: Fill the blanks so the code prints only `weekend`.
steps.explanation: `break` stops the fall-through into the next label, and `default` catches every other day. `continue` is illegal outside a loop, `yield` only works in a switch **expression**, and `else` doesn't exist in switch.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Switching on a `String` calls methods on it to find the matching case. A `null` selector throws a **NullPointerException**, even though there is a `default`. Only a `case null` label (a pattern-matching feature) avoids it.

lessons.title: switch expressions
lessons.summary: Arrow cases, yield, exhaustiveness and what fails to compile.

steps.title: A switch that returns a value

blocks.text: A **switch expression** produces a value you can assign or return. Arrow cases (`->`) never fall through, and one case can list several labels.

blocks.caption: Prints weekend

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Arrow cases behave like Python's `match`: one case runs, no fall-through. Unlike `match`, the whole switch is an expression with a value.
A switch expression must produce a value for **every possible input**, or it does not compile.

blocks.title: Statement vs expression
blocks.text: An old-style switch **statement** on an `int` may skip `default` and cover only some values. A switch **expression** may not. Check whether the switch's value is used.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The switch expression has no `default`, so it doesn't cover every `int`. A non-exhaustive switch expression is a compile error, not a runtime problem.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Every constant of `Size` has a case, so the switch expression is exhaustive and needs no `default`. `M` maps to 2.

blocks.text: An arrow case can run a block `{ }`. The block hands back its value with **`yield`**, not `return`.

blocks.caption: Prints two

items: `return` inside a switch expression: compile error.
A block that ends without `yield` (or a `throw`): compile error.
Colon-style cases also work in a switch expression; each path must `yield`, and **fall-through still happens**.

steps.prompt: Fill the blanks so the code compiles.
steps.explanation: A block in an arrow case gives its value with `yield`. `return` would try to leave the method, which a switch expression doesn't allow, and `break` can't carry a value. `default` is needed because `int` has more values than the cases cover.
This switch expression uses colon cases, so fall-through still applies. `case 1` prints `a`, has no `yield`, and falls into `case 2`, which yields 20.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Arrow cases are fine in a plain switch **statement** too, as long as each arrow is followed by a statement (`System.out.println(...)`), a block or a `throw`, not a bare value.

steps.prompt: Given `int n = 1;`, which two snippets compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Multiple labels with arrows and colon cases with `yield` are both legal. Mixing `->` and `:` fails, a block needs `yield`, and the last one has no `default`, so it isn't exhaustive.
Arrow cases never fall through, even in a switch statement and even without `break`. Only `case 1` runs, so it prints `a`.

lessons.title: Loops & labels
lessons.summary: for with commas, enhanced for, do-while, labels and infinite loops.

items: The init part may declare several variables, but only of **one type**, written once: `int i = 0, j = 5`.
`int i = 0, int j = 5` and `int i = 0, long j = 5` do not compile.
The update part may hold several expressions separated by commas: `i++, j--`.
All three parts are optional: `for (;;)` loops forever.
A variable declared in the init part is out of scope after the loop.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python's `for i in range(n)` leaves `i` usable after the loop. In Java, using the loop's `i` after the closing brace is a compile error.

The init part runs once. It is either **one** local variable declaration or a comma-separated list of **statement expressions** (assignments, method calls, `++`). You can't mix the two: `for (int i = 0, j = 1, k++; ...)` and `for (i = 0, int j = 0; ...)` don't compile.

blocks.caption: The init list assigns two variables and calls a method, once

steps.explanation: Both variables change every iteration: (0,5), (1,4), (2,3). Next would be (3,2), but `3 < 2` is false, so the loop stops after three passes.

blocks.text: The **enhanced for** loop (`for (int x : arr)`) gives you a **copy** of each element. Assigning to `x` doesn't change the array.
A **do-while** checks its condition **after** the body, so the body always runs at least once. It ends with a semicolon: `} while (cond);`.

blocks.caption: Prints 10

steps.explanation: `x` is a local copy of each element. Multiplying it changes only the copy, so the array stays `{1, 2, 3}` and the sum is 6. (`a[0] + a[1] + a[2]` is int addition, not string concatenation.)
A do-while runs the body before testing. It prints `10 `, increments `n` to 11, then `11 < 5` is false, so the loop ends and `11` prints.

steps.title: Labels: break and continue outer loops

blocks.text: A **label** is a name followed by a colon, placed right before a loop. `break` and `continue` can then target that loop instead of the innermost one.

rows: Next iteration of the innermost loop
Next iteration of the loop labeled `outer`

blocks.caption: Prints 00 10 20

blocks.title: break inside a switch
blocks.text: A plain `break` inside a `switch` that sits in a loop leaves only the **switch**, not the loop. You need a label to leave the loop from there.

steps.explanation: For i = 1 and i = 2, `j == 1` prints, then `j == 2` jumps to the next `i` (`j = 3` is never reached). For i = 3, the `break outer` check runs before the print, so the whole loop ends.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines (inside a method with `int count = 0;`) so both loops stop completely the first time `i * j == 2`, without counting that pair.
steps.explanation: The label must sit right before the outer loop, and the check must come before `count++` so the matching pair isn't counted. A plain `break` would only exit the inner loop. The result is `count == 5`.

blocks.text: If a loop's condition is the **constant** `true` and nothing `break`s out of it, the loop can never finish. Any statement after it is unreachable: compile error.

blocks.title: final makes it constant
blocks.text: `boolean on = true; while (on) {...}` is fine: `on` is a variable. But `final boolean ON = true;` is a compile-time constant, so `while (ON)` without a break makes the next statement unreachable. `return` inside the loop doesn't count as a break.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that causes the compile error.
steps.explanation: `while (true)` has no `break`; `continue` only restarts the loop. The loop can never complete, so the `println` on line 6 is unreachable, which is a compile error.

blocks.text: 11 exam-style questions on the whole unit. Most of them hinge on a single detail.

blocks.title: Exam habit
blocks.text: Check for *Compilation fails* first: a non-boolean condition, an unreachable statement, a non-constant or out-of-range case label, a non-exhaustive switch expression, or mixed `->` and `:` cases. Then trace fall-through and labels carefully.

steps.explanation: Pair each `else` with the nearest open `if`: the first `else` belongs to `if (x > 8)`, the second to `if (x > 5)`. 7 > 5 enters the outer branch, 7 > 8 is false, so `B` prints, then `D`.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Every case label must fit the selector type. A `byte` holds -128 to 127, so `case 128` doesn't compile.
String cases are compared with `equals`, which is case-sensitive. `"sun"` matches neither `"SAT"` nor `"SUN"`, so `default` yields 0.

steps.prompt: Which three types can be used as the selector of a switch with constant case labels? Choose three.
steps.explanation: Legal selectors are `char`, `byte`, `short`, `int`, their wrappers, `String` and enums. `long`, `float`, `double` and `boolean` are not.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: This is a switch **statement** (its value isn't used), so each arrow must be followed by a statement, block or `throw`. A bare `"one"` is not a statement, so it fails to compile.
i=0, 1, 3 go to `default` (+1) then `+10`. At i=2, `break` exits only the switch, so `+10` still runs. At i=4, `break loop` exits the for loop. Total: 11 + 11 + 10 + 11 = 43.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `ON` is a `final` variable with a constant initializer, so `while (ON)` is treated like `while (true)`. The loop has no `break` (`return` doesn't count), so line 6 is unreachable. Without `final`, it would compile and print nothing.
`'b'` matches `case 'b'`, so `default` is skipped even though it comes first. `b` prints, and there is no `yield`, so execution falls into `case 'c'`, which yields 3.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: A switch expression on an int needs a default to compile.
A switch statement on an int needs a default to compile.
case 1, 2: is legal in a colon-style switch.
yield can be used to leave a switch statement.
A case label can be a non-final local variable.
steps.explanation: A switch expression must be exhaustive, and for an `int` only `default` achieves that. A switch statement can skip `default`. Several labels separated by commas work with both `:` and `->`. `yield` only works in switch expressions, and labels must be constants.
The init part of a `for` may declare several variables, but the type is written only once: `int i = 0, j = 3`. Repeating `int` is a syntax error.
In a do-while, `continue` jumps to the condition check, not past it. Even numbers are skipped, so sum = 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, and the loop ends when `i < 5` is false at i = 5.
